Police responded to reports of a shooting outside a residence halls at about 01:28 local time (05:28 GMT) on Saturday. The DNC voted to approve a new calendar that bumps New Hampshire from its traditional top-two spot and leaves Iowa out for a second presidential election year. Hurricane Lala is expected to bring dangerous conditions to Hawaii this weekend, forecasters say. Multiple services have been affected by the fire in Derbyshire's Hope Valley. Security had been stepped up amid suggestions on social media of a second mass crossing on Saturday. A man who a law enforcement official says has a history of mental health issues has been arrested and charged with multiple hate crimes after disrupting Shabbat services and injuring a woman at Central Synagogue in Manhattan Friday night, New York police said. Villagers got together to encourage a cap on visitor numbers and a change to parking regulations. Iran on Saturday fired back at US President Donald Trump's claim that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz part of US territory, saying the crucial energy waterway it has blockaded "will remain Iranian".Trump told a political rally in New York state on Friday that after the US defeats Iran, "pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States". Democrats on Saturday approved dueling messages on whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished or reformed, reflecting sharp opposition to President Donald Trump's crackdown but revealing disagreement in the party ahead of the midterms. The Democratic National Committee, gathered for a summer meeting, also signed off on a raft of policy positions, including one that calls for “concrete reforms” of ICE and another for abolishing the agency that's been at the center of several fatal encounters. Michele Johnson, a DNC member from Louisiana who proposed the measure to abolish ICE, said it's time for Democrats to take a stand and pointed to the dissolution of ICE's predecessor agency, the Immigration and Naturalization Service, as a precedent. analysis.brief_en: The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) announced a multi-state oral rabies vaccine distribution campaign targeting raccoon rabies in the eastern United States. Starting in August, APHIS plans to drop millions of RABORAL V-RG® vaccine baits—coated in fishmeal and packaged in plastic sachets—across high-risk rural areas in New York, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, West Virginia, and other states. APHIS has distributed over 200 million vaccines since 1995, citing past success in reducing rabies variants, including the elimination of the dog-coyote variant in Texas in 2008. The campaign aims to prevent the raccoon variant from spreading westward into central U.S. regions.

news.source_body_en: The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) announced a multi-state oral rabies vaccine distribution campaign targeting raccoon rabies in the eastern United States. Starting in August, APHIS plans to drop millions of RABORAL V-RG® vaccine baits—coated in fishmeal and packaged in plastic sachets—across high-risk rural areas in New York, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, West Virginia, and other states. The effort follows CDC data showing 90% of rabies cases originate from wildlife. APHIS has distributed over 200 million vaccines since 1995, citing past success in reducing rabies variants, including the elimination of the dog-coyote variant in Texas in 2008. The campaign aims to prevent the raccoon variant from spreading westward into central U.S. regions.

news.content_title: Davao City records 34 human rabies deaths since 2021
news.content: Home Bacolod Cebu Davao Iloilo Manila Pampanga Tacloban Zamboanga SuperBalita SuperBalita SuperBalita Cebu SuperBalita Davao Specials Specials Videos Best of Cebu Sinulog 2026 Election 2025 Pasigarbo Palarong Pambansa TagdaKo Board Exam Results Davao Davao City records 34 human rabies deaths since 2021 CVO says Davao City recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, despite the disease being 100 percent preventable. SunStar File Photo Sun Star Davao Digital Published on: Aug 11, 2026, 2:42 pm Copied DAVAO City Veterinarian's Office (CVO) reported in a Facebook post on Monday, August 10, 2026, that the city has recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, with Calinan and Talomo districts logging the highest number of cases at six each. Based on CVO's district surveillance data, other districts also recorded human rabies deaths during the same period: Buhangin, Bunawan, Marilog, Toril, and Tugbok each recorded four cases, while Poblacion recorded two. Agdao, Baguio, and Paquibato districts recorded zero cases. The CVO said rabies remains a public health emergency despite being 100 percent preventable, noting that the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The agency attributed the deaths to gaps in responsible pet ownership, delayed vaccination, and failure to seek immediate medical attention after animal bites. ADVERTISEMENT The agency reiterated that rabies deaths can be prevented through responsible pet ownership, annual vaccination of dogs and cats, immediate washing of bite wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, prompt medical attention, completion of the recommended Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV) and Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) regimen when indicated, and reporting suspected rabid animals to authorities. Animal rabies cases In a separate post, the CVO said Davao City recorded 95 rabies-positive animal cases for CY 2025-2026 — 66 cases in 2025 and 29 cases so far in 2026. The CVO also reported 179 laboratory-confirmed animal rabies cases in Davao City from 2021 to 2026, with Talomo District logging the highest number at 67 cases, followed by Tugbok with 34 and Buhangin with 22. The agency urged pet owners to have their dogs and cats vaccinated against rabies annually, keep pets confined and supervised, avoid letting pets roam freely, and immediately report animals showing signs of rabies. ADVERTISEMENT Vaccination drive To curb the spread of the disease, the CVO has ramped up its anti-rabies vaccination program over the years. Data from the agency showed that a total of 127,503 dogs and cats were vaccinated in 2021, followed by 116,540 in 2022, 146,095 in 2023, 156,817 in 2024, and 164,125 in 2025. ADVERTISEMENT As of 2026, the CVO has already vaccinated 99,436 dogs and cats, with Talomo District accounting for the highest number of vaccinations at 31,437, followed by Buhangin with 12,931 and Toril with 10,840. The CVO said vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to prevent rabies transmission, adding that every vaccinated pet provides an added layer of protection for families and communities. In February 2026, two children aged two and four from Marilog District died of rabies after being bitten by unvaccinated animals, prompting renewed calls from health authorities for responsible pet ownership and immediate medical attention after animal bites or scratches. analysis.location_and_population: Davao City, Philippines, with specific districts such as Calinan, Talomo, Buhangin, Bunawan, Marilog, Toril, Tugbok, and Poblacion being mentioned as areas with reported cases. The affected population includes humans who were bitten by animals and did not receive timely medical attention.
analysis.event: Davao City recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, as reported by the CVO. The deaths were attributed to gaps in responsible pet ownership, delayed vaccination, and failure to seek immediate medical attention after animal bites.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: A total of 34 human rabies deaths were confirmed in Davao City from 2021 to 2026. The CVO noted that rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, emphasizing the public health emergency status. Additionally, 179 laboratory-confirmed animal rabies cases were reported during the same period, with Talomo District having the highest number of cases.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CVO has been actively reporting rabies cases and deaths, emphasizing the need for responsible pet ownership, annual vaccination of dogs and cats, immediate medical attention after animal bites, and reporting suspected rabid animals. The agency has also ramped up its anti-rabies vaccination program to curb the spread of the disease.

analysis.brief_en: Davao City has recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, according to the Davao City Veterinarian's Office (CVO). The deaths were reported in a Facebook post on August 10, 2026, with Calinan and Talomo districts having the highest number of cases at six each. Other districts such as Buhangin, Bunawan, Marilog, Toril, and Tugbok also reported cases, with Poblacion having two. The CVO emphasized that rabies is 100% preventable but remains a public health emergency due to gaps in responsible pet ownership, delayed vaccination, and failure to seek immediate medical attention after animal bites. In 2026, two children from Marilog District died of rabies after being bitten by unvaccinated animals, prompting renewed calls for preventive measures. The CVO has been conducting an anti-rabies vaccination program, with over 99,436 dogs and cats vaccinated as of 2026. Talomo District recorded the highest number of vaccinations, followed by Buhangin and Toril. The agency reiterated that vaccination is one of the most effective ways to prevent rabies transmission and urged pet owners to keep their animals confined and report suspected rabid animals to authorities.

news.content_zh: 据达沃市兽医办公室 (CVO) 称,2021 年至 2026 年,达沃市已记录了 34 例确诊的人类 狂犬病 死亡事件。2026 年 8 月 10 日,Facebook 发布了一篇帖子,报告了死亡病例,其中卡利南 (Calinan) 和塔洛莫 (Talomo) 地区的病例数最多,各有 6 例。布杭金、布纳万、马里洛格、托里尔和图格博克等其他地区也报告了病例,其中波布拉西翁有两例。CVO 强调,狂犬病 是 100% 可预防的,但由于负责任的宠物主人存在差距、延迟 狂犬病 以及动物咬伤后未能立即寻求医疗救助,狂犬病 仍然是公共卫生紧急情况。2026 年,马里洛格区的两名儿童被未接种疫苗的动物咬伤后死于 狂犬病,促使人们再次呼吁采取预防措施。CVO 一直在开展抗 狂犬病 疫苗接种 计划,截至 2026 年,已有超过 99,436 只狗和猫接种了疫苗。塔洛莫区的 狂犬病 疫苗接种 数量最多,其次是布杭金 (Buhangin) 和托里尔 (Toril)。该机构重申,疫苗接种 是预防 狂犬病 传播 的最有效方法之一,并敦促宠物主人限制其动物,并向当局报告可疑的狂犬病动物。

Pop.Life GOOD LIFE OHAYO PINAS Pets Last updated August 15, 2026, 8:26 PM Rabies and Anti-Rabies Vaccinations: A Historical and Contemporary Perspective with Focus on the Philippines By Mariana Burgos August 15, 2026, 7:50 PM Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp A cat is vaccinated against rabies at the vet clinic. Photo from iStock royalty-free images.) Resize Text:16px Estimated reading time: 3 minutes and 5 seconds First of two parts Rabies, a fatal viral disease affecting the central nervous system, has haunted humanity and animals for centuries. Its history is as old as recorded medicine, but the journey toward effective treatment and prevention is a remarkable story of scientific innovation and public health progress. - Advertisement - Discover more Newspaper advertising space Philippine public affairs City & Local Guides The History of Rabies and the Birth of Vaccination Rabies has been known since antiquity, described in ancient texts as a terrifying illness transmitted through animal bites, primarily from dogs. The disease causes severe neurological symptoms and is almost invariably fatal once clinical signs appear. The turning point in rabies treatment came in 1885, when Louis Pasteur, the renowned French chemist and microbiologist, developed the first rabies vaccine. According to the article “The history of the first rabies vaccination in 1885” by Institut Pasteur, Pasteur’s breakthrough involved using dried spinal cords from infected rabbits to create a weakened form of the virus. This vaccine was first administered to a young boy named Joseph Meister, who had been bitten multiple times by a rabid dog. The successful treatment of Meister marked the dawn of modern immunization against rabies. Further elaborating on this, the article “How the Modern Rabies Vaccine Came to Be” from History Of Vaccines.org highlights that Pasteur’s method laid the foundation for subsequent vaccine development. Early vaccines were nerve tissue-based, derived from infected animal tissues, but these had limitations in safety and efficacy. Close-up shot of an anti-rabies vaccine in a vet clinic. (Photo from iStock royalty-free images.) Development of Rabies Vaccines for Humans and Animals Over time, rabies vaccines evolved significantly. The World Health Organization (WHO) now recommends cell culture vaccines, which are safer and more effective than the older nerve tissue vaccines. These vaccines are produced using purified virus grown in cell cultures, reducing adverse reactions and improving immune response. The article “Rabies vaccines – Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases” by WHO explains that two main types of vaccines protect humans: nerve tissue vaccines (largely phased out) and cell culture vaccines. Vaccination protocols include pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for those bitten or exposed to potentially rabid animals. For animals, particularly dogs which are the primary source of human rabies infections, vaccination campaigns have been critical. Mass dog vaccination reduces the reservoir of the virus, thereby protecting human populations indirectly. Latest Developments in Rabies Vaccination Recent scientific advances are reshaping rabies vaccination strategies. According to the article “Developments in rabies vaccines” published on PMC by NIH, researchers are exploring novel vaccine formulations including recombinant vaccines, adjuvanted vaccines, and modified live vaccines that enhance immune response and durability. A notable innovation described in the article “New single-dose, temperature-stable rabies vaccines could expand global access” by CU Boulder engineers involves a single-dose vaccine with timed-release technology. This could revolutionize rabies prevention by simplifying vaccination schedules and improving vaccine stability in resource-limited settings. Additionally, the Cleveland Clinic’s article “Rabies Vaccine: Benefits & Side Effects” underscores that while current vaccines are highly effective, breakthrough infections can occur, emphasizing the need for continued vigilance and vaccine improvements. Rabies in the Philippines: Current Situation and Challenges The Philippines remains one of the countries most affected by rabies in Asia. According to the Philippine News Agency’s report “PH records 400 annual rabies deaths, 4M animal bite cases,” the country experiences approximately 300 to 400 human rabies deaths yearly, with millions of animal bite incidents recorded. Children and impoverished communities are disproportionately affected. The Lancet Regional Health article “Rabies in the Philippines: a call to action” highlights a worrying increase in rabies cases in recent years despite ongoing control efforts. Pop.Life GOOD LIFE OHAYO PINAS Pets Last updated August 15, 2026, 8:26 PM Rabies and Anti-Rabies Vaccinations: A Historical and Contemporary Perspective with Focus on the Philippines By Mariana Burgos August 15, 2026, 7:50 PM Share Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp A cat is vaccinated against rabies at the vet clinic. Photo from iStock royalty-free images.) Resize Text:16px Estimated reading time: 3 minutes and 5 seconds First of two parts Rabies, a fatal viral disease affecting the central nervous system, has haunted humanity and animals for centuries. Its history is as old as recorded medicine, but the journey toward effective treatment and prevention is a remarkable story of scientific innovation and public health progress. - Advertisement - Discover more Newspaper advertising space Philippine public affairs City & Local Guides The History of Rabies and the Birth of Vaccination Rabies has been known since antiquity, described in ancient texts as a terrifying illness transmitted through animal bites, primarily from dogs. The disease causes severe neurological symptoms and is almost invariably fatal once clinical signs appear. The turning point in rabies treatment came in 1885, when Louis Pasteur, the renowned French chemist and microbiologist, developed the first rabies vaccine. According to the article “The history of the first rabies vaccination in 1885” by Institut Pasteur, Pasteur’s breakthrough involved using dried spinal cords from infected rabbits to create a weakened form of the virus. This vaccine was first administered to a young boy named Joseph Meister, who had been bitten multiple times by a rabid dog. The successful treatment of Meister marked the dawn of modern immunization against rabies. Further elaborating on this, the article “How the Modern Rabies Vaccine Came to Be” from History Of Vaccines.org highlights that Pasteur’s method laid the foundation for subsequent vaccine development. Early vaccines were nerve tissue-based, derived from infected animal tissues, but these had limitations in safety and efficacy. Close-up shot of an anti-rabies vaccine in a vet clinic. (Photo from iStock royalty-free images.) Development of Rabies Vaccines for Humans and Animals Over time, rabies vaccines evolved significantly. The World Health Organization (WHO) now recommends cell culture vaccines, which are safer and more effective than the older nerve tissue vaccines. These vaccines are produced using purified virus grown in cell cultures, reducing adverse reactions and improving immune response. The article “Rabies vaccines – Control of Neglected Tropical Diseases” by WHO explains that two main types of vaccines protect humans: nerve tissue vaccines (largely phased out) and cell culture vaccines. Vaccination protocols include pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for those bitten or exposed to potentially rabid animals. For animals, particularly dogs which are the primary source of human rabies infections, vaccination campaigns have been critical. Mass dog vaccination reduces the reservoir of the virus, thereby protecting human populations indirectly. Latest Developments in Rabies Vaccination Recent scientific advances are reshaping rabies vaccination strategies. According to the article “Developments in rabies vaccines” published on PMC by NIH, researchers are exploring novel vaccine formulations including recombinant vaccines, adjuvanted vaccines, and modified live vaccines that enhance immune response and durability. A notable innovation described in the article “New single-dose, temperature-stable rabies vaccines could expand global access” by CU Boulder engineers involves a single-dose vaccine with timed-release technology. This could revolutionize rabies prevention by simplifying vaccination schedules and improving vaccine stability in resource-limited settings. Additionally, the Cleveland Clinic’s article “Rabies Vaccine: Benefits & Side Effects” underscores that while current vaccines are highly effective, breakthrough infections can occur, emphasizing the need for continued vigilance and vaccine improvements. Rabies in the Philippines: Current Situation and Challenges The Philippines remains one of the countries most affected by rabies in Asia. According to the Philippine News Agency’s report “PH records 400 annual rabies deaths, 4M animal bite cases,” the country experiences approximately 300 to 400 human rabies deaths yearly, with millions of animal bite incidents recorded. Children and impoverished communities are disproportionately affected. The Lancet Regional Health article “Rabies in the Philippines: a call to action” highlights a worrying increase in rabies cases in recent years despite ongoing control efforts. news.content_zh: Bing News RSS 于 2026 年 8 月 15 日发表的文章“狂犬病 和反 狂犬病 狂犬病:聚焦菲律宾的历史和当代视角”概述了 狂犬病(一种影响中枢神经系统的致命病毒性疾病)以及通过 疫苗接种 进行预防。它强调了路易斯·巴斯德 (Louis Pasteur) 在 1885 年使用受感染兔子的干燥脊髓制成的第一个 狂犬病 疫苗 的历史发展。本文还讨论了现代 疫苗 类型,例如细胞培养 疫苗,它比旧的基于神经组织的 疫苗 更安全、更有效。它强调了大众狗疫苗接种在减少狂犬病传播和保护人类群体方面的重要性。菲律宾被认为是亚洲受 狂犬病 影响最严重的国家之一。本文没有报告具体的 暴发 细节、病例数或死亡人数,而是重点关注 狂犬病 预防和 疫苗 发展的更广泛背景。来源是一篇笼统的文章,没有详细说明具体的调查或风险评估。

news.content: Medscape AI News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape Canada Rabies in an 11-Year-Old Boy After Bat Contact Michael van den Heuvel August 13, 2026CMAJ. 2026;198(25):E969-E972.doi:10.1503/cmaj.251933 4 111 Add to Email Alerts Key Takeaway Exposure to a bat without a visible bite wound, nonspecific symptoms, and an initial misdiagnosis: What begins as what appears to be a herpes infection develops into fulminant encephalitis within a few days. The case published in the CMAJ of an 11-year-old boy from Canada illustrates how deceptive the course of rabies can be — and why any direct contact with a bat must be medically evaluated. The Patient and His Medical History The patient is 11 years old, immunocompetent, and had been healthy. When his parents brought him to the emergency department of a municipal hospital in Ontario, Canada, he complained of painful difficulty swallowing and vomiting. The boy had no known allergies and no tick bites and had not traveled abroad. There were no known infected contacts. The symptoms began about a week earlier: Initially, the boy felt tingling and numbness on the right side of his face. The symptoms worsened; he lost his appetite and later developed swelling on the right side of his face. Four days after the onset of symptoms, the family visited an emergency department for the first time. There, doctors suspected Bell palsy, likely associated with a herpes simplex infection. The boy was prescribed valacyclovir, 1 g three times a day. However, due to severe pain when swallowing, he was barely able to take the medication. It was only during further discussion that the parents told the doctors in the emergency room about an incident they had not previously considered dangerous: 19 days before the onset of symptoms, the family had been at a vacation home in northern Ontario. During the night, the boy woke up because a bat was perched on his nose and mouth. He reflexively swatted the animal away. His father caught the bat and released it outside. Because there were no visible bite or scratch wounds on the child’s face and the bat did not appear abnormal in the parents’ assessment, the family did not seek medical help at the time. SUGGESTED FOR YOU Findings During the examination in the emergency room, the boy did not appear to be seriously ill overall. His vital signs were largely within the normal range; the only notable finding was tachycardia at 134 beats/min. Neurologically, there were mild sensory disturbances in the distribution area of the right trigeminal nerve. In addition, the doctors noted mucosal ulcers on the upper and lower gums. Further neurologic and oropharyngeal examinations initially revealed no significant findings. There was no clear facial nerve palsy at this time. The facial swelling described earlier was also no longer visible. Laboratory results also did not provide a clear picture: Electrolytes, glucose, and creatinine were within the normal range. The complete blood count was unremarkable except for leukocytosis and is consistent with an inflammatory process. Initial Presumptive Diagnosis Due to the mucosal changes and neurologic symptoms, doctors initially suspected severe herpetic gingivostomatitis with Bell palsy. On the basis of the history of contact with a bat, the emergency physician notified the local health department to evaluate the need for postexposure rabies prophylaxis. However, the boy was initially discharged with a suspected diagnosis of herpetic gingivostomatitis. The next morning, his parents brought him back to the emergency department. His condition had now deteriorated significantly. He exhibited right-sided facial weakness, increasing sensory disturbances, and slurred speech. He was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. However, tachycardia was again noted, this time at 139 beats/min. Under the working diagnosis of severe herpes gingivostomatitis with Bell palsy, the boy was admitted to the hospital. He was given intravenous acyclovir and prednisone. While he was still waiting to be admitted, his condition deteriorated dramatically: He had fever of up to 39.1 °C, difficulty swallowing, confusion, and visual hallucinations. A CT scan of the head revealed no abnormalities. However, the disease progressed rapidly. By that evening, multiple cranial nerve deficits appeared, including signs of bulbar palsy. This was accompanied by pronounced hypersalivation. To protect his airway, the boy was intubated and transferred to the pediatric ICU. Further Diagnostics In the ICU, the history of bat exposure took center stage. The combination of direct contact to the face, sensory deficits, cranial nerve involvement, dysphagia, hypersalivation, and encephalopathy now made rabies a suspected diagnosis. However, the treatment team also considered, as part of the differential diagnosis, more common pathogens of infectious encephalitis, including the herpes simplex virus, enteroviruses, or the West Nile virus. Noninfectious causes were also taken into account, such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, autoimmune encephalitis, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. In parallel with general infectious disease diagnostics, samples were collected for rabies testing: serum, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), saliva, and a skin biopsy from the neck area. Saliva and neck skin samples, in particular, were considered especially important specimens when rabies is suspected. The CSF findings were consistent with viral inflammation of the central nervous system (CNS). Lymphocytic pleocytosis was observed with leukocyte count of 272 cells/μL, 88% of which are lymphocytes. Protein was significantly elevated at 1.22 g/L, whereas glucose level was normal at 3.5 mmol/L. MRI of the brain revealed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem, particularly in the medulla oblongata. Additional changes were found in the left caudate nucleus, in cortical gray matter — with confluence in the right posterior temporal and occipital lobes — as well as in the cervical spinal cord. These findings were not specific, but they were consistent with a suspected case of rabies. On the fourth day of hospitalization, polymerase chain reaction testing of saliva samples finally confirmed the diagnosis. Further testing identified a bat-associated variant of the rabies virus. It was therefore clear that the infection was related to the nocturnal contact at the vacation home, even though there was no visible bite wound. Treatment Even before the diagnosis was confirmed, the boy received targeted anti-infective therapy. To address both bacterial and viral causes of encephalitis, the team treated him with intravenous ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir. After the positive rabies test, it became clear that the disease had already reached a stage at which there is no longer any established causal therapy. Treatment focused on intensive care support: securing the airway, ventilation, stabilizing circulation, and managing neurologic and autonomic complications. Nevertheless, the team was exploring experimental options. Among other things, the doctors discussed the intraventricular administration of rabies immunoglobulin via an Ommaya reservoir: a small, dome-shaped plastic reservoir implanted under the scalp. It is connected to a cerebral ventricle via a thin catheter. This would require neurosurgical intervention. Due to the invasive nature of the procedure, the lack of proven efficacy, and the rapidly progressing neurologic damage, the family, together with the treatment team, decided against this option. An experimental gene therapy using an adeno-associated viral vector designed to express a neutralizing antibody was also considered but not pursued: The therapy was not available in the short term, its efficacy has not been proven, and the boy’s clinical condition was deteriorating rapidly. Severe complications subsequently arose. The patient developed autonomic dysregulation, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and progressive neurologic deficits. By the 5th day of hospitalization, brainstem reflexes were no longer detectable. On the 17th day of treatment, following discussions with the family, life-sustaining measures were discontinued. Discussion This case illustrates why rabies remains one of the most feared infectious diseases. Once neurologic symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Although isolated survivors have been documented worldwide, they remain exceptions. Many patients are left with severe neurologic damage. There is no established therapy that is effective after the onset of symptoms. The route of infection is particularly insidious in this case. The boy has no visible wound. There is no visible bite, no scratch, and no bleeding. Nevertheless, direct contact between the bat and the boy’s face, nose, and mouth is apparently sufficient to assume significant exposure. In North America, bats are an important reservoir for human rabies infections. Their bites can be so small that they go unnoticed. In Europe, too, bats can transmit rabies viruses. However, unlike in the US, these are usually not the classic rabies virus but closely related European bat lyssaviruses. These belong to the same viral genus and also cause a fatal disease. The clinical course also demonstrates how easily rabies can be overlooked at first. The early symptoms are nonspecific: tingling, numbness, loss of appetite, and difficulty swallowing, followed later by fever and neurologic deficits. Paresthesias beginning in the face and facial nerve involvement may initially suggest a herpes infection or Bell palsy. The mucosal ulcers in the mouth are also more consistent with gingivostomatitis than with rabies; in retrospect, they may have been caused by trauma resulting from the sensory disturbance. It is only the rapid neurologic deterioration that points to the correct diagnosis. A typical feature is the spread of the virus along peripheral nerves into the CNS. Because the presumed site of entry is in the facial region, this explains the early involvement of trigeminal and facial structures. The later symptoms, including dysphagia and hypersalivation, are also consistent with this course of the disease. A CT scan of the head may be unremarkable. MRI findings are possible but nonspecific; they frequently involve the brainstem, spinal cord, or basal ganglia. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein levels, and normal glucose levels. Multiple samples are required to confirm the diagnosis, including saliva, a nuchal skin biopsy, serum, and CSF. Negative results do not definitively rule out rabies if the clinical presentation is consistent with the disease. The most important therapeutic measure remains prevention. Postexposure prophylaxis involving thorough wound cleansing, rabies immunoglobulin, and vaccination is highly effective when administered in a timely manner before the onset of neurologic symptoms. This case demonstrates that the problem is not the lack of effective prevention but rather the failure to recognize relevant exposure. The message for clinical practice is clear: In cases of any progressive neurologic symptoms, physicians should specifically inquire about contact with bats or other potentially rabid animals and, when in doubt, immediately initiate postexposure prophylaxis. Treatment focused on intensive care support: securing the airway, ventilation, stabilizing circulation, and managing neurologic and autonomic complications. Nevertheless, the team was exploring experimental options. Among other things, the doctors discussed the intraventricular administration of rabies immunoglobulin via an Ommaya reservoir: a small, dome-shaped plastic reservoir implanted under the scalp. It is connected to a cerebral ventricle via a thin catheter. This would require neurosurgical intervention. Due to the invasive nature of the procedure, the lack of proven efficacy, and the rapidly progressing neurologic damage, the family, together with the treatment team, decided against this option. An experimental gene therapy using an adeno-associated viral vector designed to express a neutralizing antibody was also considered but not pursued: The therapy was not available in the short term, its efficacy has not been proven, and the boy’s clinical condition was deteriorating rapidly. Severe complications subsequently arose. The patient developed autonomic dysregulation, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and progressive neurologic deficits. By the 5th day of hospitalization, brainstem reflexes were no longer detectable. On the 17th day of treatment, following discussions with the family, life-sustaining measures were discontinued. Discussion This case illustrates why rabies remains one of the most feared infectious diseases. Once neurologic symptoms appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Although isolated survivors have been documented worldwide, they remain exceptions. Many patients are left with severe neurologic damage. There is no established therapy that is effective after the onset of symptoms. The route of infection is particularly insidious in this case. The boy has no visible wound. There is no visible bite, no scratch, and no bleeding. Nevertheless, direct contact between the bat and the boy’s face, nose, and mouth is apparently sufficient to assume significant exposure. In North America, bats are an important reservoir for human rabies infections. Their bites can be so small that they go unnoticed. In Europe, too, bats can transmit rabies viruses. However, unlike in the US, these are usually not the classic rabies virus but closely related European bat lyssaviruses. These belong to the same viral genus and also cause a fatal disease. The clinical course also demonstrates how easily rabies can be overlooked at first. The early symptoms are nonspecific: tingling, numbness, loss of appetite, and difficulty swallowing, followed later by fever and neurologic deficits. Paresthesias beginning in the face and facial nerve involvement may initially suggest a herpes infection or Bell palsy. The mucosal ulcers in the mouth are also more consistent with gingivostomatitis than with rabies; in retrospect, they may have been caused by trauma resulting from the sensory disturbance. It is only the rapid neurologic deterioration that points to the correct diagnosis. A typical feature is the spread of the virus along peripheral nerves into the CNS. Because the presumed site of entry is in the facial region, this explains the early involvement of trigeminal and facial structures. The later symptoms, including dysphagia and hypersalivation, are also consistent with this course of the disease. A CT scan of the head may be unremarkable. MRI findings are possible but nonspecific; they frequently involve the brainstem, spinal cord, or basal ganglia. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein levels, and normal glucose levels. Multiple samples are required to confirm the diagnosis, including saliva, a nuchal skin biopsy, serum, and CSF. Negative results do not definitively rule out rabies if the clinical presentation is consistent with the disease. The most important therapeutic measure remains prevention. Postexposure prophylaxis involving thorough wound cleansing, rabies immunoglobulin, and vaccination is highly effective when administered in a timely manner before the onset of neurologic symptoms. This case demonstrates that the problem is not the lack of effective prevention but rather the failure to recognize relevant exposure. The message for clinical practice is clear: In cases of any progressive neurologic symptoms, physicians should specifically inquire about contact with bats or other potentially rabid animals and, when in doubt, immediately initiate postexposure prophylaxis. analysis.event: An 11-year-old boy from Canada developed rabies after a direct contact with a bat, which was initially misdiagnosed as a herpes infection and Bell palsy. The diagnosis was confirmed through polymerase chain reaction testing of saliva samples.

analysis.brief_en: An 11-year-old boy from Canada developed rabies after a direct contact with a bat during a vacation in northern Ontario. The symptoms began about a week earlier, initially presenting as tingling and numbness on the right side of his face, which later worsened to include difficulty swallowing, vomiting, and facial swelling. The initial diagnosis was suspected to be a herpes infection and Bell palsy, leading to treatment with valacyclovir. However, due to the severity of his condition, the emergency physician notified the local health department to evaluate the need for postexposure rabies prophylaxis. The boy was admitted to the hospital and later intubated and transferred to the pediatric ICU after his condition deteriorated significantly. Polymerase chain reaction testing of saliva samples confirmed the rabies diagnosis, and the infection was linked to the bat contact, even though there were no visible bite wounds. Experimental treatment options were considered but not pursued due to lack of availability and proven efficacy. The case highlights the deceptive nature of rabies and the importance of medical evaluation following any direct contact with bats.

news.content_zh: 一名来自加拿大的 11 岁男孩在安大略省北部度假期间直接接触蝙蝠后患上了 狂犬病。症状大约在一周前开始,最初表现为右侧脸刺痛和麻木,后来恶化,包括吞咽困难、呕吐和面部肿胀。最初的诊断被怀疑是疱疹感染和贝尔麻痹,导致治疗使用伐昔洛韦。然而,由于病情严重,急诊医生通知当地卫生部门评估是否需要进行暴露后狂犬病预防。男孩被送入医院,后来病情明显恶化后插管并转入儿科重症监护室。对唾液样本的聚合酶链反应测试证实了 狂犬病 诊断,并且感染与蝙蝠接触有关,尽管没有可见的咬伤。考虑了实验性 治疗 选项,但由于缺乏可用性和经过验证的功效而没有采用。该案例凸显了 狂犬病 的欺骗性,以及在与蝙蝠直接接触后进行医学评估的重要性。

The situation remains under investigation, with no indication of a broader outbreak or specific risk levels being communicated to the public.

Topics: Diseases and Conditions, Rabies, Welfare and Industry Share Favorite Please login to bookmark Close Please login to access. ADVERTISEMENT The CDC identified the virus as the skunk variant rabies. | Adobe Stock The Kentucky Department for Public Health (KDPH) was notified on July 28, 2025, of a confirmed rabies case in a 21-year-old American Quarter Horse gelding. The horse had a clinical history that included one month of weight loss and one week of anorexia. On July 24, the horse was evaluated at a veterinary clinic for agitation and photosensitivity and returned the following day exhibiting aggression and a high fever. The horse, which had not been vaccinated against rabies, was euthanized on July 25. Postmortem specimens were sent to the University of Kentucky Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory where diagnostic testing confirmed rabies, and the CDC later identified the virus as the skunk variant rabies. This case underscores the ongoing risk of rabies in Kentucky, where 24 equine cases have been identified since 1989. While the owner did not report observing wildlife on the property, recent trends show an uptick in skunk variant rabies in the south-central region of the state, highlighting the often-unseen risk posed by wildlife reservoirs. In Kentucky, both skunk and bat variants circulate, and horses may be exposed through direct contact with bites or scratches from infected animals. The Kentucky Department for Public Health worked with local environmental health officials to quickly identify and contact individuals who may have been exposed to the infected horse. Post-exposure treatment is effective but is time-sensitive and costly. Thirteen people were assessed, including 12 veterinary staff and one community member. Of these, nine were determined to have high-risk exposures and were advised to receive rabies post exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Rabies PEP for humans typically includes immediate wound cleansing (if a wound is present), administration of human rabies immune globulin (if not previously vaccinated) and a series of rabies vaccinations on Days 0, 3, 7 and 14. Animal health measures were also enacted. Two unvaccinated equine pasture mates were identified as exposed and placed under a 180-day strict quarantine by the Kentucky Department of Agriculture. No additional domestic or livestock exposures were identified. In this case, the Kansas State three dose PEP animal protocol was implemented, with vaccines administered on Days 0, 7 and 21–28 for the two exposed horses. This case highlights the critical importance of rabies vaccination in horses. Rabies is a universally fatal and completely preventable disease. Rabies is a core vaccine recommended annually for all equids by the American Association of Equine Practitioners. Infected unvaccinated animals not only face a horrific death but also pose a significant risk to human health. Vaccinating all of our domestic animals against rabies protects our families in addition to protecting our animals. While preventing this disease by vaccination is paramount, quarantine considerations, particularly for the performance horse, can also be significant. If a rabid skunk were found in a horse paddock, unvaccinated horses in that paddock would be subject to 180 days of quarantine, as compared to 45 days for vaccinated horses. This is an excerpt from Equine Disease Quarterly, Vol. 35, Issue 3, funded by Equus/Standardbred Station Inc. and M&J Insurance. It was written by Allison Siu, DVM, MPH, CDC career epidemiology field officer at the Kentucky Department for Public Health, in Frankfort, and Kelly Giesbrecht, DVM, MPH, Dipl. AVOHS, Kentucky state public health veterinarian also with the Kentucky Department for Public Health. ADVERTISEMENT The CDC identified the virus as the skunk variant rabies. | Adobe Stock The Kentucky Department for Public Health (KDPH) was notified on July 28, 2025, of a confirmed rabies case in a 21-year-old American Quarter Horse gelding. The horse had a clinical history that included one month of weight loss and one week of anorexia. On July 24, the horse was evaluated at a veterinary clinic for agitation and photosensitivity and returned the following day exhibiting aggression and a high fever. The horse, which had not been vaccinated against rabies, was euthanized on July 25. Postmortem specimens were sent to the University of Kentucky Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory where diagnostic testing confirmed rabies, and the CDC later identified the virus as the skunk variant rabies. This case underscores the ongoing risk of rabies in Kentucky, where 24 equine cases have been identified since 1989. While the owner did not report observing wildlife on the property, recent trends show an uptick in skunk variant rabies in the south-central region of the state, highlighting the often-unseen risk posed by wildlife reservoirs. In Kentucky, both skunk and bat variants circulate, and horses may be exposed through direct contact with bites or scratches from infected animals. The Kentucky Department for Public Health worked with local environmental health officials to quickly identify and contact individuals who may have been exposed to the infected horse. Post-exposure treatment is effective but is time-sensitive and costly. Thirteen people were assessed, including 12 veterinary staff and one community member. Of these, nine were determined to have high-risk exposures and were advised to receive rabies post exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Rabies PEP for humans typically includes immediate wound cleansing (if a wound is present), administration of human rabies immune globulin (if not previously vaccinated) and a series of rabies vaccinations on Days 0, 3, 7 and 14. Animal health measures were also enacted. Two unvaccinated equine pasture mates were identified as exposed and placed under a 180-day strict quarantine by the Kentucky Department of Agriculture. No additional domestic or livestock exposures were identified. In this case, the Kansas State three dose PEP animal protocol was implemented, with vaccines administered on Days 0, 7 and 21–28 for the two exposed horses. This case highlights the critical importance of rabies vaccination in horses. Rabies is a universally fatal and completely preventable disease. Rabies is a core vaccine recommended annually for all equids by the American Association of Equine Practitioners. Infected unvaccinated animals not only face a horrific death but also pose a significant risk to human health. Vaccinating all of our domestic animals against rabies protects our families in addition to protecting our animals. While preventing this disease by vaccination is paramount, quarantine considerations, particularly for the performance horse, can also be significant. If a rabid skunk were found in a horse paddock, unvaccinated horses in that paddock would be subject to 180 days of quarantine, as compared to 45 days for vaccinated horses. This is an excerpt from Equine Disease Quarterly, Vol. 35, Issue 3, funded by Equus/Standardbred Station Inc. and M&J Insurance. It was written by Allison Siu, DVM, MPH, CDC career epidemiology field officer at the Kentucky Department for Public Health, in Frankfort, and Kelly Giesbrecht, DVM, MPH, Dipl. news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 11 日报道的肯塔基州一匹 21 岁美国夸特马骟马中确诊的 狂犬病 病例凸显了该疾病的持续风险。2025年7月24日,这匹马接受了躁动和光敏性评估,并在肯塔基大学兽医诊断实验室通过尸检证实其患有狂犬病后,于2025年7月25日被安乐死。疾病预防控制中心将该病毒鉴定为臭鼬变种。这匹马尚未接种疫苗,该案例凸显了马 狂犬病 疫苗接种 的重要性。对 9 个人(包括 12 名兽医人员和 1 名社区成员)进行了暴露评估,并建议接受 狂犬病 暴露后预防 (PEP)。两只未接种疫苗的马匹被隔离 180 天。没有发现额外的家庭或牲畜暴露。该病例反映了肯塔基州的一个更广泛的趋势,自 1989 年以来,该州已报告了 24 例马 狂犬病 病例。狂犬病 是一种普遍致命且可预防的疾病,PEP 有效,但时间敏感且成本高昂。肯塔基州公共卫生部与当地官员合作控制局势,强调 疫苗接种 保护动物和人类健康的必要性。

news.content_title: St. Lawrence County confirms three more rabies cases
news.content: WSYR St. Lawrence County confirms three more rabies cases Dan Mount 16 hours ago CANTON, N.Y. (WWTI) – The New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Laboratory has confirmed rabies cases in one bat and two raccoons in St. Lawrence County. The new positive results bring the total number of confirmed rabies cases in the county to 14 this year. The infected bat was found in Gouverneur and submitted for testing by the St. Lawrence County Public Health Department. The two raccoons were located in DeKalb and Oswegatchie and submitted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Rabies is a deadly virus transmitted through the saliva or brain tissue of infected animals, most commonly spread through bites or scratches. Wild animals that most frequently carry the virus include raccoons, skunks, bats and foxes. Domestic animals, including cats and dogs, can also contract the virus after coming into contact with rabid wildlife. Here are some tips offered by the county’s public health department to combat the spread of the disease: ● Report all animal bites or possible rabies exposures to St. Lawrence County Public Health at (315) 386-2325. ● If a bat is found in a home or other occupied space, carefully capture it in a container without making direct contact, and contact SLCPHD. Retaining the bat for testing is important because it can help determine whether rabies exposure occurred and whether treatment is necessary. ● Keep pets and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations, including indoor cats. ● Supervise pets outdoors and feed them indoors. ● Avoid feeding, touching, or adopting wild animals or stray pets. ● Wash any bite or scratch wounds immediately and seek medical attention if exposed to a suspected rabid animal. ● Reduce attractions for wildlife by securing garbage, compost, birdseed, and pet food. ● Contact an animal control officer if a wild animal is living near your home. ● If your pet or livestock may have been exposed to a rabid animal, contact your veterinarian and Public Health immediately. Wild animals may be submitted for rabies testing if they have had contact with humans or pets, or if they display unusual behavior. If possible, safely contain the animal for testing and report the incident to Public Health. For more information about rabies prevention, visit the St. Lawrence County Rabies Control Program or call the St. Lawrence County Public Health Department at (315) 386-2325. The Harford County Health Department said Tuesday it had received confirmation from state health officials that two animals -- a raccoon and a fox -- had tested positive for the rabies virus. The rabid raccoon was found near the 200 block of Cooley Mill Road in Havre de Grace, while the rabid fox was found near the 700 block of Walters Mill Road in Forest Hill, Maryland. The health department said the rabid animals may have exposed people or pets in surrounding areas. "Witnessing a raccoon, fox, or other wildlife is not cause for alarm," the department said in a statement. "But if you or your pets have had contact with a raccoon or fox near the specified areas, please call the Harford County Health Department at 410-877-2300 for follow-up." Anne Arundel bat alert In Anne Arundel County, an alert was issued by the health department seeking information about anyone who might have come in contact with an infected bat found outside Almondbury Drive in Pasadena. A statement said the bat was found Aug. 9 and tested positive for rabies. The Arundel County Department of Health is urging anyone who might have come into contact with the bat to contact the department at 410-222-7254. Area residents who discover unexplained wounds on their pets should also reach out to report the injuries. Rabies is spread by the bite or scratch of an infected animal, such as a groundhog, cat, fox, raccoon, skunk or bat. It is also spread when an infected animal's saliva comes in contact with the eyes, nose, mouth or open cut of a person or another animal. Latest warnings follow recent biting incidents Preventive treatment might be required for anyone who handled, fed or was attacked by the infected animals. Rabies is a fatal disease, and preventive treatment (injections) must be started as soon as possible. The latest reports of rabid animals follows an incident in July in which a beaver infected with rabies bit a 13-year-old boy at Cunningham Falls State Park in Maryland's Frederick County. news.content_original: Latest U.S. Iran War Mangione Plea World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Baltimore | News Weather Sports Video On WJZ 88° Local Maryland Best of WJZ at 9 Politics Consumer Business Health Entertainment First Alert Weather Radar & Maps Closings/Delays Weather Watchers All Sports CBS Sports HQ Ravens Orioles Terps College Sports Horse Racing Golf Odds WJZ at 9 Community MVP Volunteer with WJZ WJZ and the Baltimore Banner HealthyMD WJZ Investigates Black History Month About Us Meet The Team Contact Us Share A News Tip Links & Numbers Nominate An MVP Advertise With Us Download The App Watch CBS News Local News Rabies alerts issued in Harford, Anne Arundel counties involving raccoon, bat and fox By Bryan Lynn Updated on: August 12, 2026 / 8:26 PM EDT / CBS Baltimore Add CBS News on Google Health officials in Harford and Anne Arundel counties have issued new rabies alerts involving a raccoon, a fox and a bat. The Harford County Health Department said Tuesday it had received confirmation from state health officials that two animals -- a raccoon and a fox -- had tested positive for the rabies virus. The rabid raccoon was found near the 200 block of Cooley Mill Road in Havre de Grace, while the rabid fox was found near the 700 block of Walters Mill Road in Forest Hill, Maryland. The health department said the rabid animals may have exposed people or pets in surrounding areas. "Witnessing a raccoon, fox, or other wildlife is not cause for alarm," the department said in a statement. "But if you or your pets have had contact with a raccoon or fox near the specified areas, please call the Harford County Health Department at 410-877-2300 for follow-up." Anne Arundel bat alert In Anne Arundel County, an alert was issued by the health department seeking information about anyone who might have come in contact with an infected bat found outside Almondbury Drive in Pasadena. A statement said the bat was found Aug. 9 and tested positive for rabies. The Arundel County Department of Health is urging anyone who might have come into contact with the bat to contact the department at 410-222-7254. Area residents who discover unexplained wounds on their pets should also reach out to report the injuries. Rabies is spread by the bite or scratch of an infected animal, such as a groundhog, cat, fox, raccoon, skunk or bat. It is also spread when an infected animal's saliva comes in contact with the eyes, nose, mouth or open cut of a person or another animal. Latest warnings follow recent biting incidents Preventive treatment might be required for anyone who handled, fed or was attacked by the infected animals. Rabies is a fatal disease, and preventive treatment (injections) must be started as soon as possible. The latest reports of rabid animals follows an incident in July in which a beaver infected with rabies bit a 13-year-old boy at Cunningham Falls State Park in Maryland's Frederick County. The boy sustained injuries to his hands and chest and was flown to Johns Hopkins Hospital for treatment. Then, earlier this month, a 19-year-old man was bitten on the leg while visiting Cunningham Falls State Park. analysis.brief_en: Jones County, Iowa, issued a public health warning after confirming a rabies case in a stray kitten. The confirmation came from the Jones County Public Health Department, which reported the case between Morley and Anamosa. Rabies, a viral disease spread through saliva, primarily via bites, is a serious concern for both humans and animals. The department advised residents to avoid handling stray animals, especially if they appear sick or behave unusually, and to wash any wounds immediately. They also recommended consulting a veterinarian if pets are bitten or exhibit strange behavior. The warning emphasizes the importance of keeping pets up to date on rabies vaccinations. The situation is currently under investigation, with no specific case or death counts provided in the report. The public health department is actively communicating the risks and necessary precautions to the community.

news.content: The Vineyard Gazette - Martha's Vineyard News | Island Bat is First Confirmed Rabies Case Since 2019 Skip to main content Browse Subscribe Directory Real Estate Classifieds Store Visit Martha's Vineyard Martha's Vineyard Magazine Island Weddings The Vine Cook the Vineyard Sections News Opinion Arts & Entertainment Calendar Nature & Science Obituaries Podcasts Photography Island Information Time Machine Towns Aquinnah Chilmark Edgartown Oak Bluffs Vineyard Haven West Tisbury Accounts Search form Search View Archive Brown bats are common the the Vineyard. A dead bat that tested positive for rabies was found in a Tisbury home. Courtesy Luanne Johnson News Island Bat is First Confirmed Rabies Case Since 2019 Ethan Genter Wednesday, August 12, 2026 - 10:30am Print 0 Comments A dead bat that a cat brought into a Tisbury home last month tested positive for rabies, according to town health officials. This is the first documented rabies case on the Vineyard since 2019 and only the second going back to when testing began in 1985. Health officials said there is little cause for concern as it appears to be an isolated incident. “If we find a series of tests that come back positive we will start to monitor the situation,” Drew Belsky, Tisbury health agent, told the Gazette this week. The bat was discovered by the homeowners in mid-July, according to Heather Maciel, the Tisbury animal control officer. The cat that found the bat, as well as two other cats living at the home, were all put into a 45-day quarantine and seem to be doing fine, she said. The homeowners also took precautionary doses of the rabies vaccine, health officials said. Tisbury regularly sends off about six bats a year to the Massachusetts state public health laboratory for testing. After this bat was found to test positive, two more dead bats were found and tested. Both of the latter bats tested negative. Rabies is a viral disease that is deadly if people don’t receive medical care before symptoms start. It primarily is spread through bites or scratches from an infected animal. Bats are one of the main animals that can catch and pass on rabies, along with skunks, raccoons and foxes. Health officials encourage people to see a doctor if they come into contact with a bat because bat bites or scratches can be tiny and hard to detect. The bat that tested positive was a brown bat, according to Ms. Maciel, the same species that tested positive in 2019 in Tisbury. analysis.event: A dead brown bat tested positive for rabies, the first confirmed case on Martha's Vineyard since 2019, reported by town health officials.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: One confirmed rabies case in a bat; no human or animal cases reported; three cats quarantined for 45 days; two additional bats tested negative; risk described as low and isolated.

analysis.brief_en: A dead brown bat found in a Tisbury home in mid-July tested positive for rabies, marking the first confirmed case on Martha’s Vineyard since 2019, according to local health officials. The bat, discovered by homeowners, was brought inside by a cat, prompting the quarantine of three cats for 45 days; all remain healthy. Health authorities emphasized the incident appears isolated and noted that two additional bats tested negative. news.content_zh: 据当地卫生官员称,7 月中旬在蒂斯伯里 (Tisbury) 的一处住宅中发现的一只死棕色蝙蝠的 狂犬病 检测结果呈阳性,这是玛莎葡萄园岛 (Martha’s Vineyard) 自 2019 年以来首例确诊病例。房主发现的蝙蝠是由一只猫带入室内的,导致三只猫被隔离 45 天;所有人都保持健康。卫生当局强调这起事件似乎是孤立的,并指出另外两只蝙蝠的检测结果呈阴性。官员们敦促居民如果暴露在外,请立即就医,因为蝙蝠咬伤很难被发现。常规蝙蝠测试仍在继续,只有在出现多个阳性病例时才会计划加强监测。

analysis.brief_en: On August 14, 2026, St. Lawrence County, New York, confirmed three new human rabies cases, according to the county’s Public Health Department. The announcement, reported by WWNY 7 News, marks the first documented human rabies cases in the county this year. Health authorities have not disclosed additional details regarding the patients, potential exposures, or transmission routes. The confirmation follows standard laboratory testing protocols for rabies lyssavirus. While the source of infection is under investigation, public health officials have not issued specific guidance or warnings beyond confirming the cases. Further updates are expected as the investigation progresses.

supplementary_news.content: Home Bacolod Cebu Davao Iloilo Manila Pampanga Tacloban Zamboanga SuperBalita SuperBalita SuperBalita Cebu SuperBalita Davao Specials Specials Videos Best of Cebu Sinulog 2026 Election 2025 Pasigarbo Palarong Pambansa TagdaKo Board Exam Results Davao Davao City records 34 human rabies deaths since 2021 CVO says Davao City recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, despite the disease being 100 percent preventable. SunStar File Photo Sun Star Davao Digital Published on: Aug 11, 2026, 2:42 pm Copied DAVAO City Veterinarian's Office (CVO) reported in a Facebook post on Monday, August 10, 2026, that the city has recorded 34 confirmed human rabies deaths from 2021 to 2026, with Calinan and Talomo districts logging the highest number of cases at six each. Based on CVO's district surveillance data, other districts also recorded human rabies deaths during the same period: Buhangin, Bunawan, Marilog, Toril, and Tugbok each recorded four cases, while Poblacion recorded two. Agdao, Baguio, and Paquibato districts recorded zero cases. The CVO said rabies remains a public health emergency despite being 100 percent preventable, noting that the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The agency attributed the deaths to gaps in responsible pet ownership, delayed vaccination, and failure to seek immediate medical attention after animal bites. The agency reiterated that rabies deaths can be prevented through responsible pet ownership, annual vaccination of dogs and cats, immediate washing of bite wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, prompt medical attention, completion of the recommended Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV) and Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) regimen when indicated, and reporting suspected rabid animals to authorities. Animal rabies cases In a separate post, the CVO said Davao City recorded 95 rabies-positive animal cases for CY 2025-2026 — 66 cases in 2025 and 29 cases so far in 2026. The CVO also reported 179 laboratory-confirmed animal rabies cases in Davao City from 2021 to 2026, with Talomo District logging the highest number at 67 cases, followed by Tugbok with 34 and Buhangin with 22. The agency urged pet owners to have their dogs and cats vaccinated against rabies annually, keep pets confined and supervised, avoid letting pets roam freely, and immediately report animals showing signs of rabies. Vaccination drive To curb the spread of the disease, the CVO has ramped up its anti-rabies vaccination program over the years. Data from the agency showed that a total of 127,503 dogs and cats were vaccinated in 2021, followed by 116,540 in 2022, 146,095 in 2023, 156,817 in 2024, and 164,125 in 2025. As of 2026, the CVO has already vaccinated 99,436 dogs and cats, with Talomo District accounting for the highest number of vaccinations at 31,437, followed by Buhangin with 12,931 and Toril with 10,840. The CVO said vaccination remains one of the most effective ways to prevent rabies transmission, adding that every vaccinated pet provides an added layer of protection for families and communities. In February 2026, two children aged two and four from Marilog District died of rabies after being bitten by unvaccinated animals, prompting renewed calls from health authorities for responsible pet ownership and immediate medical attention after animal bites or scratches.
